paper_title: Ego2Act: Evaluating Goal-Directed Manipulation in Egocentric Video Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Video generation models are increasingly being explored as world simulators for embodied planning and learning. To do so effectively, these models must not only generate visually appealing frames, but also predict how environments dynamically evolve when executing goal-directed actions. While evaluating these capabilities is crucial, existing benchmarks focus mainly on single short actions or step-by-step instructions. This leaves multi-step physical reasoning underexplored, especially in egocentric video generation that requires planning to simulate proper execution to accomplish high-level goals by carrying out multiple real-world manipulations. We introduce Ego2Act, a goal-directed benchmark featuring 2,640 videos from 110 real-world tasks across day-to-day settings, varying object clutter and multi-step complexity. Given an initial scene image and a high-level goal, Ego2Act evaluates whether video generation models can produce realistic egocentric videos of a hand manipulating objects to carry out the task. To support scalable evaluation, we also introduce Ego2ActJudge, a reference-free evaluation pipeline that achieves better task completion and physics plausibility evaluation alignment with human consensus compared to relevant baselines. Our findings reveal that models' generated simulations often skip or partially execute steps, leaving later steps missing dependent states, which leads to unfulfilled goal. Furthermore, models consistently fail at fine-grained physical dynamics, particularly during complex object manipulation and persistent world modeling. We hope Ego2Act provides a rigorous testbed for advancing video models toward physically plausible, goal-directed simulation.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recent advances in video generation have produced models capable of generating complex visual scenes and dynamic motion with better physical and world consistency (Team Wan et al., 2025; Kong et al., 2024; OpenAI, 2024). Building on these foundations, researchers are exploring these models as embodied world simulators to support agents planning and learning, such as generating manipulation demonstrations for robot training (Jang et al., 2025) or predicting action outcomes for embodied planning (Bagchi et al., 2026). However, effective agent learning requires video rollouts that are functionally valid, i.e., actions successfully reach the goal while executing sequence of correct physical state changes. Evaluating these rollouts is challenging because goal-directed prompts state only the target outcome, leaving intermediate action sequences unspecified. Since multiple valid action paths can reach the goal, evaluation cannot rely on reference videos and must also verify physical constraints across diverse possibilities. The trajectories share an initial scene and goal, with highlighted task and physics errors along each execution. outcome (Du et al., 2023; 2024; Bagchi et al., 2026). Consider an egocentric task in Figure 1, where model has to generate demonstration of packing capped toothpaste tube and folded toothbrush into travel case. The toothpaste can be capped before or after the toothbrush is folded, but both items must be prepared and packed before the case is closed. Evaluating such open-ended execution is challenging across video generation, but becomes especially demanding in egocentric settings where models must precisely track fine-grained object states through frequent hand occlusions and dynamic camera motion. However, existing benchmarks fall short of evaluating such scenarios. Some evaluate complex demonstrations in exocentric settings (Yang et al., 2026), which bypasses the fine-grained handobject interaction dynamics, end-effector occlusions, and dynamic view shifts native to egocentric perspectives. Conversely, existing egocentric benchmarks fail to evaluate autonomous planning, since they either evaluate generation with fidelity metrics rather than goal completion (Shen et al., 2026) or their metrics rely on explicit, step-by-step prompt guidance (Rong et al., 2026; Wei et al., 2026). Consequently, they lack high-level, goal-directed task prompts required to test whether models can independently plan, execute, and track complex multi-step state transitions. To address this gap, we formulate two key research questions: RQ1: Goal-directed egocentric manipulation capabilities. To what extent can state-of-theart video models generate physically valid egocentric manipulation videos to reach target goal from an initial scene? RQ2: Reference-free scalable evaluation. How can we automate the evaluation of openended goal execution, in agreement with human judgement, without relying on ground-truth reference videos? To address RQ1, we introduce EGO2ACT, goal-directed video generation benchmark that tests video models ability to generate complete, physically plausible executions of everyday egocentric tasks. EGO2ACT consists of 110 real-world cases spanning diverse actions, domains, environmental clutter, and horizons, totaling 2,640 videos across 660 human-collected real videos and 1,980 model-generated outputs. Each case pairs real-world starting scene with high-level goal, requiring more than five steps on average that successful human executions take median of 20.4 seconds. While identifying these failures provides critical insights into model limits, manually detecting such subtle, easily missed errors in open-ended manipulation videos is not trivial and scalable even for human annotators. To enable automatic evaluation at scale and answer RQ2, we further introduce EGO2ACTJUDGE, reference-free, rubric-derived automated evaluator that assesses task completion and physical plausibility. Under human inspection on our subset panel, Seedance-2.0, the highest-scoring model, achieves an overall score of only 64.0 points, exposing critical gap for future studies to bridge. We demonstrate evaluation reliability through high inter-annotator rubric agreement (ICC = 0.86) and strong alignment between EGO2ACTJUDGE and human consensus (r = 0.69) outperforming relevant baselines. We summarize our main contributions below: 1. We introduce EGO2ACT, to our knowledge, the first benchmark for goal-directed, multistep egocentric video generation, comprising 110 real-world cases and 2,640 videos spanning diverse domains, environmental clutter, and action complexities. 2. We propose EGO2ACTJUDGE, reference-free evaluation pipeline for open-ended manipulation rollouts that assesses task completion and physical plausibility, outperforming existing automated baselines in human alignment. 3. We present comprehensive analysis of rubric design, model failure modes in egocentric physical execution, and the overall reliability of the proposed automated evaluation.

sections.title: 2.1 VIDEO GENERATION FOR EMBODIED TASKS
sections.content: Generative video models are increasingly utilized as embodied world simulators and predictive planners. Early frameworks adapt video generation to different control modalities: UniSim (Yang et al., 2024) simulates visual outcomes from low-level actions, UniPi (Du et al., 2023) optimizes goalconditioned policies in video space, and VLP (Du et al., 2024) performs tree search over generated video futures for multi-step planning. Recent works scale policy learning data by extracting robot trajectories in DreamGen (Jang et al., 2025) or forecasting motor-conditioned egocentric rollouts in EgoWM (Bagchi et al., 2026). Most related to our setup, EgoForge (Shen et al., 2026) generates first-person rollouts from initial scenes and instructions. In parallel, benchmarks like ALFRED (Shridhar et al., 2020) and CALVIN (Mees et al., 2022) test interactive agents in simulators, while EgoTV (Hazra et al., 2023) verifies pre-recorded videos using subtask graphs. Whereas simulator agents and video checkers evaluate fixed interactions or pre-recorded traces, EGO2ACT assesses whether video models can generate complete and physically plausible multi-step task execution given real-world egocentric initial scene image and the desired high-level final goal.

sections.title: 2.2 EVALUATING ACTIONS FROM VIDEO MODELS
sections.content: General video evaluation frameworks like VBench (Huang et al., 2024) and VideoScore (He et al., 2024) focus on visual quality and prompt alignment, but fail to verify subgoal progress in multistep execution. VideoPhy-2 (Bansal et al., 2026) and PQSG (Pothiraj et al., 2026) evaluate physical and logical adherence. Embodied benchmarks assess instruction following and physics in DreamGen (Jang et al., 2025) and WorldModelBench (Li et al., 2025), multi-step planning in RBench (Deng et al., 2026), action simulation in WR-Arena (PAN Team et al., 2026), general world model capabilities in WoW-World-Eval (Fan et al., 2026), and robotic execution in RoboWMBench (Jiang et al., 2026). While EgoForge (Shen et al., 2026) shares our generation interface, it is generation method rather than benchmark, and it is evaluated with reference-based visual fidelity metrics rather than goal completion. In contrast, EGO2ACT evaluates multi-step goal completion and its physical accuracy, which EGO2ACTJUDGE automates directly without requiring reference trajectories. In summary, we outline the novelty of EGO2ACT in Table 1.

sections.title: 3.1 TASK DEFINITION
sections.content: Given an initial scene image f1 and goal prompt G, EGO2ACT measures whether video models can generate physically plausible embodied video sequence = {f1, f2, . . . , fT } that executes the task using only items visible in f1. The benchmark primarily evaluates two evaluation axes. (1) Task completion verifies that generated sequence performs the intermediate steps needed to arrive at goal state G. (2) Physical plausibility assesses whether hand-object contacts, object persistence under occlusion, and state changes stay realistic throughout execution. Since only outlines the target outcome without prescribing any ground truth sequence, any rollout reaching the goal under plausible physics counts as successful. EGO2ACT is scored by human raters and EGO2ACTJUDGE, following the protocol in Section 4.

sections.title: 3.2 DATA COLLECTION PIPELINE
sections.content: To construct EGO2ACT, we manually collect real-world scenes and human task recordings, then annotate their environments, complexity, and execution features. Each case includes 6 human recordings: 3 successful attempts with distinct action sequences and 3 unsuccessful attempts as controls. We also prompt 6 video models to generate 3 videos across different trials (seeds), resulting in 18 generated videos per case. The final benchmark contains 110 cases, with 660 human recordings and 1,980 generated videos, totaling 2,640 videos. Task features and data statistics. The benchmark spans five task categories: kitchen and food preparation, household organization and storage, personal care and utilities, office and study workspace, and other everyday activities. We assign annotators to category, then ask them to propose task conforming to this. We then verify the appropriateness of the proposed task and discard examples violating our requirements as outlined in Appendix A.1. Scenes cover three clutter levels: none, minimal, and heavy, which annotators assign by judging the amount of task-irrelevant content visible in the initial scene. Each case pairs an initial scene image f1 with an outcomeoriented goal that specifies the desired result without prescribing intermediate steps. We verify that each case admits at least 3 distinct execution sequences across its human recordings. Sequences are considered distinct if they differ in either: (1) sub-action sequencing (e.g. washing mug before wiping the counter vs. wiping first), (2) resource or tool selection (e.g. using sponge vs. paper towel), or (3) intermediate state transitions (e.g. storing an item in drawer vs. placing it on shelf). Appendix A.1 provides detailed construction criteria and operational definitions. Human recordings and verification. Human recordings must maintain an egocentric perspective, record with sufficient brightness, and follow the closed-world constraint. Objects may move out of view during execution, but no additional objects can be introduced. Human recordings violating this constraint are excluded. Before including case, annotators review its goal definition clarity and outcome-oriented wording, task feasibility, absence of duplicate tasks, and metadata accuracy. They then inspect the human recordings for visual quality, viewpoint and orientation consistency, and compliance with the collection constraints. sections.title: 4 EGO2ACTJUDGE
sections.content: We build EGO2ACTJUDGE based on human-crafted rubrics to construct multi-stage VQA evaluation pipeline. Operating without training or reference trajectories, the evaluator receives video and goal to output score triplet of (task score , physics score , final score S). The overall pipeline is illustrated in Figure 3, with full rubrics, scoring rules, and pipeline implementation details provided in Appendix B. Below, we formalize the four primary stages of this evaluation pipeline. (1) Subgoals. Given goal and scene f1 derived from without viewing the whole video, EGO2ACTJUDGE identifies minimal set of observable subgoals = {g1, . . . , gN }, where each subgoal involves one source object, at most one target, and one action. For example, moving object to location is single valid subgoal, whereas moving and together to is split due to multiobject definition on one side. Although the plan is re-derived for every video, it is largely stable: 91% of plans keep the same subgoal count and they name nearly the same objects (Appendix G). (2) Task completion. For each subgoal gi, the judge evaluates task execution through three gates, binary checks applied in order until one fails (early exit): T1 whether action initiation occurs, T2 whether the coarse-level interaction process takes place, and T3 whether the post-process state matches the desired outcome. Evaluation halts at the first failed gate, producing discrete score ti {0, 1, 2, 3}, the number of gates passed. We compute the task completion score as the mean across subgoals, = 1 i=1 ti. Appendix B.1 details the task rubric and gate criteria. (cid:80)N (3) Physics Plausibility. For each subgoal gi, we assess physical validity independently of task success across four gates: P1 state and object continuity, P2 physically valid causation at interaction onset, P3 plausible contact during the interaction process, and P4 post-interaction physical stability. Scoring halts at the first failed gate, yielding discrete score pi {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}. An unattempted subgoal (ti = 0) involves no physical interaction, so it is marked unattempted (N/A) rather than scored. The physics score is averaged only over the set of evaluated subgoals via = 1 iJ pi, which is undefined when is empty. Appendix B.2 details the physical plausibility rubric and operational rules. Evaluation on EGO2ACT reveals video models capability gap relative to human execution.As shown in Table 2, proprietary models lead, with Seedance-2.0 scoring highest on aggregate. Among openweight models, MiniMax-H3 remains competitive, which we attribute to its larger parameter scale and providerside prompt expansion. We analyze this rewriting behavior through dedicated prompt ablation study in Appendix E.4, finding that while prompt expansion can boost performance for certain models, its benefits do not reliably generalize across architectures. On per-aspect score relations (Figure 4a), there is moderate positive correlation between both axes, but the wide spread of points highlights large per-sample variance, indicating that task success and physical accuracy do not strictly track one another. sections.title: 5.3 QUALITATIVE ANALYSIS OF SIMULATION FAILURES
sections.content: To ground our fine-grained action analysis, we highlight recurring task and physics failure modes across model rollouts, where each error category corresponds to its matching color accent in Figure 11, with an extended set of comprehensive samples provided in Appendix F. Skipped prerequisites (a) recur when videos proceed to later operations, or cut diTask errors. rectly to completed state, without completing dependency actions. Models use capped objects, attempt insertion before opening containers, or pour before correctly orienting the receiving vessel. Incomplete outcomes (b) happens when models attempt an operation but fail to reach the intended final state. Objects remain partly outside containers, surface markings persist after wiping, or components not completely attached. Precision-sensitive actions also produce same errors, including misplaced lines, unequal partitions, and inaccurate pours. Domain-specific operations (c) involving less familiar objects or culturally specific artifacts often results incomplete outcomes. Models manipulate the relevant parts but fail to establish the relations needed for correct operation, suggesting limited understanding of how these objects function together. Physics errors. Object inconsistencies (d) affect both object state and count. In terms of state, objects undergo unexplained changes in shape, material, identity, or assembly, sometimes transforming into different items. In terms of count, objects appear, disappear, duplicate, or merge without cor-

sections.title: 5.4 RUBRIC & AUTOMATED JUDGE ABLATIONS
sections.content: We test sequential gating in two ways: by rescoring fixed pilot human annotations with recorded gate decisions, bypassing each gate or scoring all gates independently and comparing with holistic human ratings (Figure 5), and by rerunning EGO2ACTJUDGE with independent gates (Appendix G). Gated Evaluation Prevents Score Inflation. As shown in Figure 5, removing the primary physics continuity gate (P1) leads to large error increase, while bypassing the task initiation gate (T1) similarly degrades alignment. Similar observations apply to other gates, though early crucial gating has the largest impact. Scoring all gates independently instead of sequentially also raises error, sharply for physics and slightly for task. The same holds inside EGO2ACTJUDGE. Rerunning it with every gate asked independently inflates Final scores by 6.8 points and lowers Final from 0.69 to 0.65 and CCC from 0.62 to 0.51 (Appendix G). Our key takeaway is that strict sequential gating makes fine-grained rubric scores more consistent with human judgment, and we expect it to help VLM judges (1) localize each sub-aspect of rubric evaluation and (2) explain each pass or exit decision. sections.content: We present EGO2ACT and EGO2ACTJUDGE to evaluate whether generative video models are able to generate goal-directed egocentric manipulation rollouts that complete the task with plausible physics. Addressing RQ2 (Reliable & scalable evaluation), EGO2ACTJUDGE provides reference-free, rubric-derived pipeline that achieves Pearson correlation of = 0.69 with human consensus. Conclusively, EGO2ACT demonstrates that modern video generators struggle to align physical accuracy with complete task execution, underscoring the need for future world model building that is able to (1) execute every required step rather than omitting prerequisite states or leaving actions incomplete, (2) maintain persistent object identity and state under dynamic egocentric motion and frequent hand occlusions, and (3) ground contact-rich interactions in physically plausible dynamics to serve as reliable simulators for embodied planning.

sections.title: AI USAGE DISCLOSURE
sections.content: In this work, we used generative AI tools for method implementation (coding assistants helped write and edit the evaluation and analysis code), dataset reformatting (consolidating evaluator outputs into analysis tables), and qualitative data analysis support (drafting the per-recording metadata of observed sub-actions, involved objects, and action types, which annotators then checked and corrected). We have not used generative AI tools for synthetic dataset generation, theoretical or conceptual framework development, mathematical claims, proofs, hypothesis proposal or refinement, research methodology or experiment design feedback, translation, or result interpretation. Additionally, we used generative AI tools for figure creation (plotting code for the dataset-statistics figure), readability editing and structure suggestions for the manuscript, and reference formatting. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: all reported numbers are reproduced by the released analysis scripts from the stored evaluator outputs and human annotations, AI-drafted metadata was checked against the recordings, and all text was reviewed and edited by the authors. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

sections.title: REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT
sections.content: We document every component needed to reproduce our results. Appendix A.1 gives the taskconstruction and verification criteria, and Appendix A.4 gives the exact prompt, seeds, and settings used to generate every video, with the models and durations in Section 5.1. Appendix gives the full human Task and Physics rubrics, including the gate definitions and the handling of unattempted and unobservable subgoals. Appendix B.5 specifies the EGO2ACTJUDGE backbone, decoding and frame-sampling settings, pseudocode, and all prompts verbatim (Appendix B.6). Appendix C.1 specifies how each baselines outputs are mapped to Task and Physics scores, and Appendix C.2 lists every change made to run the baselines, including the Simple VQA and adapted RBench prompts. Appendix describes the human-annotation protocol, including annotator calibration, and the agreement and alignment metrics. All reported tables and figures are computed by analysis scripts from the stored per-video judge outputs, baseline outputs, and human ratings, without additional model calls. We will release the benchmark (initial scenes, goals, human recordings, and generated videos), the EGO2ACTJUDGE code and prompts, the human annotations and rubric guidelines, and the analysis scripts upon publication.

sections.title: ETHICS STATEMENT
sections.content: EGO2ACT contains egocentric recordings made by nine annotators in everyday indoor settings, which show the annotators hands and household objects from first-person view, together with videos generated from these scenes through the model providers interfaces. All annotators gave informed consent to the recording, annotation, and release of their recordings. The three raters in the human study scored anonymized videos without knowing which model produced them. We remove location and device metadata from released images and videos, and the recordings are intended to contain no faces or other personally identifying content. EGO2ACT and EGO2ACTJUDGE evaluate existing video models, and we release no new generator. Realistic manipulation videos could be misused to depict events that did not happen, and stricter judge of physical plausibility could make such videos harder to detect, so we release the benchmark and evaluator for research use.

A.2 FEATURE DETAILS Each EGO2ACT case consists of an initial scene, goal, six human recordings, and the eighteen videos generated from that scene, together with features that describe the task. Annotators begin by manually assigning the domain, clutter level, and task-relevant objects for each case. To generate the remaining features, such as step counts and trajectory descriptions, we prompt vision-language model (VLM) to analyze frames sampled from successful recordings.

Domain Definition Example objects Kitchen and food preparation Preparing, serving, or storing food and drink, and handling or cleaning the tableware and utensils used for them. Keys, toy cars, shoe boxes, storage boxes, trash cans, pillows, garments and laundry bags, candles and lighters, clocks, remote controls, and light bulbs. Office and study workspace Personal care and utilities Others Setting up, organizing, or using items on desk for work or study, including stationery, books, and electronic devices with their accessories. Laptops, keyboards, mice, books, notebooks, pens, markers, highlighters, erasers, staplers, scissors, calculators, headphones, and chargers. Handling hygiene, grooming, and health items, and packing personal belongings into pouches or bags outside an office or study context. Toothbrushes, toothpaste tubes, pouches and bags, eye drops, lipsticks, makeup jars, cotton pads, spray bottles, face wash tubes, and bandages. Everyday activities outside the four domains above, such as handling musical instruments, footwear, money, or games. Guitars, shoes and sandals, backpacks, wallets, banknotes and coins, board-game pieces, matryoshka dolls, and tennis rackets. Media formats. The initial scene is resized to 512 pixels on its longer side with the aspect ratio preserved, and the same resized image is given to the video models and to EGO2ACTJUDGE. Human recordings are captured as MP4 or MOV files. Both the human recordings and the generated videos are resized to 480p, that is, at most 854 480 pixels, and the baseline evaluators receive them as H.264 MP4 files at no more than 24 fps. EGO2ACTJUDGE instead samples frames from each video and resizes every frame to 512 pixels on its longer side (Appendix B.5). Steps and objects. step is purposeful operation that is visible in recording, such as moving an object, opening lid, or pouring, and single motion that carries two objects together counts as one step. The trajectory description lists these steps with their approximate times, and the number of steps counts them. Because both describe how one recording was executed, the number of steps can vary across the three successful recordings of case and does not measure the minimum number of subgoals that the goal requires. The object list is provided by the annotator as part of the case, whereas the involved objects are the solid objects actually handled in the successful recordings, together with objects that receive another object, such as container. Objects that are never used are not counted as involved objects, which keeps the object count separate from the clutter level. Action families. Each action type belongs to one of the nine action families defined in Table 7, and case covers the families of all of its action types. For example, case in which the recordings attach ball to stick, stand the stick upright, and stack two cans covers attachment and connection (A4), shape and orientation change (A5), and relocation and arrangement (A1). Figure 2b shows how often two families appear in the same case, and Figure 2f counts the distinct families per case. A.3 COLLECTION WORKFLOW & ANNOTATION PROTOCOL Annotators and case proposal. The data are collected by nine annotators. Each annotator is assigned one of the five task categories and proposes cases within it, capturing the initial scene for each proposed case. Before collection, annotators receive an illustrated guideline that explains every requirement of the rubric in Appendix A.1 with accepted and rejected example scenes and goals. Every proposed case is checked against the rubric, and cases that violate any requirement are revised or discarded. Clutter is left to the annotators discretion during capture and is labeled afterwards as none, minimal, or heavy according to the amount of task-irrelevant content visible in the initial scene.

ID Action family Definition A1 Relocation A2 Containment A3 Opening / closing A4 Attachment A5 A6 Shape / orientation Transfer / mixing A7 Surface treatment A8 Cutting A9 Device activation Moving an object to new position or arranging objects relative to one another (place, move, stack, align, sort). Putting an object into container or enclosure, or taking it out (insert, remove, pack, retrieve). Changing whether container, lid, cap, or latch is open or closed (open, close, cap, uncap, latch). Joining two objects into lasting connection, such as attaching part or plugging in cable, or undoing such connection (attach, plug in). Changing the shape or orientation of an object (turn upright, fold, flip). Moving liquid or granular material from one place to another, or mixing materials (pour, dispense, scoop, stir). Acting on the surface of an object to clean it or change its markings (wipe, scrub, erase). Dividing an object into separate parts (cut, break). Operating control that changes the state of device (switch on, switch off, ignite). Recording. All the recordings of case start from the state shown in the initial scene and keep the same firstperson viewpoint and orientation. Each recording must also be sufficiently bright and respect the closed-world constraint. sections.content: Each generated video is evaluated against the initial egocentric scene, the task goal, and the associated subgoal decomposition. Evaluation is reference free: raters do not compare the video with canonical execution. The rubric separates task completion from physical plausibility, since video may satisfy the goal while containing physically implausible interactions, or exhibit plausible interactions while failing to complete the task. This section details the rubrics summarized in Section 4. It condenses the illustrated annotation guidelines given to human raters, the Task Completion rubric and the Physical Aspects rubric, which will be released with the benchmark. We distinguish their annotation guidance from the judges operational interpretation where necessary. Appendix B.5 specifies the executable procedure, evidence tools, and unavailable-output policy. B.1 TASK-COMPLETION RUBRIC Given goal G, annotators first decompose it into atomic subgoals {S1, . . . , SN }. Each subgoal contains one source object, at most one target, and one principal action. For each subgoal Si, annotators check three gates in order and stop at the first gate that fails (early exit): 1. T1 Intent. Is there visible task-directed behavior involving the correct object, tool, or mechanism? If not, ti = 0. 2. T2 Process. Is the intended action carried out as recognizable high-level trajectory from initiation to completion? If not, ti = 1. 3. T3 Final state. Does the subgoal end in the state specified by the goal? If not, ti = 2, and otherwise ti = 3. The subgoal score therefore counts the gates passed before the first failure, ti = max{k {0, 1, 2, 3} : gates T1, . . . , Tk all pass}, so later gate is never checked once an earlier one fails. sections.title: C DETAILED BASELINE SETUP
sections.content: C.1 TASK/PHYSICS MAPPING DECISIONS Different evaluators operationalize different constructs, so we map only components whose semantics overlap the current Task or Physics rubric. All mappings below are fixed and non-fitted. We retain each methods official native output separately, map selected components to 0100 from their nominal endpoints, and never replace an unsupported axis with zero. Thus these proxies support within-evaluator cohort comparisons, but they do not make score levels interchangeable across evaluator rows. In Table 2, Ori. is each benchmarks original final score averaged over videos, and VideoScore, which has no official final score, uses the mean of its five aspects.

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Reference annotation. The Human column aggregates the three annotators ratings (Appendix D). Task uses the mean 03 task score, mapped by 100s/3. Physics uses the conditional mean of observed 04 subgoal-window ratings, mapped by 100s/4, and an unobserved Physics window remains unavailable instead of contributing zero. WR-Arena. WR-Arenas Action Simulation Fidelity evaluates whether the rollout realizes the instructed action and outcome on its native 03 scale (PAN Team et al., 2026). We therefore map it to Task by 100s/3. It exposes no separate component that tests object identity, visible causal contact, during-interaction plausibility, and post-interaction stability as required by our Physics rubric, so Physics is unsupported. PQSG. PQSG decomposes prompt into object-existence, action-verification, and physics questions linked by scene graph (Pothiraj et al., 2026). For each video, we map the mean binary actionverification response to Task and the mean binary physics response to Physics, then multiply each by 100. Object-existence nodes are excluded: mere presence does not establish Task completion and does not test the identity continuity or causal interaction required by Physics. This component view is diagnostic, while the dependency-weighted official PQSG final score remains intact in the native report. RBench. The RBench common-manipulation evaluator reports action execution, task completion, object consistency, hand consistency, and physical plausibility on 15 scales (Deng et al., 2026). Task is the mean of action execution and task completion, matching process execution and the intended terminal state. Physics is the mean of object consistency, hand consistency, and physical plausibility, covering identity continuity and visible interaction coherence. Both means use 25(s1) to map 15 to 0100. The upstream gated RBench total is preserved separately and is not substituted for either axis. WorldModelBench. WorldModelBench separately scores instruction following, five physical-law checks, and two common-sense checks (Li et al., 2025). Instruction following maps to Task by 100s/3. Physics is the mean pass rate over the five physical-law checks plus temporal consistency, or 100(slaws + stemporal)/6. The aesthetics check is excluded because visual appeal is outside both rubrics, and the official 010 total remains native score rather than an axis proxy. VideoScore. VideoScore predicts visual quality, temporal consistency, dynamic degree, text-tovideo alignment, and factual consistency on nominal 14 scales (He et al., 2024). Text-to-video alignment is the closest available Task component. Physics uses the mean of temporal and factual consistency, which captures the closest observable subset of stable, plausible evolution. Visual quality and dynamic degree are excluded because polish and motion magnitude do not imply either completion or physical correctness. Selected heads are mapped by 100(s1)/3, and raw predictions are not clipped when the regression model slightly exceeds its nominal range. C.2 MODIFICATION COURTESY We run every baseline from its pinned official release and keep its native output and scoring rule. sections.content: D.1 STUDY PROTOCOL Subset construction. The benchmark contains 110 cases. Each case provides six human-recorded control videos and 18 generated videos, corresponding to six generation models and three random seeds per model. We select 25-case evaluation subset with five cases per task category, yielding 600 videos in total. Selection is performed at the case level. Clutter labels cover all 25 cases, but only one case is Heavy. Once case is selected, all of its control and generated videos are included, preventing within-case selection bias and preserving the complete modelseed structure. Human annotation. Three annotators score the subset using the rubric in Section 4. Two are PhD students at university (aged 23 and 25), and the third (aged 34) is working professional with fluent reading and writing proficiency in English. Videos are assigned anonymously and without generator names, so annotators are blind to the model that produced each video, and each video is assigned to up to three annotators. Before annotation, each annotator completes an individual calibration session, meeting that walks through the rubric and resolves questions, followed by scoring five sample videos that include human controls and span different levels of physics errors. Annotators provide task-completion score on 03 scale and physics-accuracy score on 04 scale. Physics is marked N/A when the criterion is not applicable, and such entries are treated as missing and are not converted to zero. For each video and rubric dimension, the human reference label is the arithmetic mean of the available valid ratings. The human Final score is the geometric mean of the two axis means, and video with mean Task rating of 0 receives Final score of 0, matching the rule for EGO2ACTJUDGE. We retain the individual ratings for reliability analysis. Agreement metrics. We report agreement both among human annotators and between automated evaluators and the human reference labels. For humanhuman agreement, we report the one-way random-effects intraclass correlation coefficient of the average rating, estimated by REML, Lins concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), interval Krippendorffs α, mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean squared error (RMSE). For automated-evaluator alignment, each evaluator is compared with the aggregated human reference using the same metrics. Task completion and physics accuracy are analyzed separately, and an overall score is reported only as secondary summary of the two dimensions. Uncertainty and aggregation. To account for correlations among videos from the same case, confidence intervals are estimated with case-level bootstrap resampling. Specifically, we resample the 25 cases with replacement, include all videos belonging to each sampled case, and recompute every metric for 1,000 bootstrap replicates. We report the point estimate and the two-sided 95% percentile

The dominant levels motivate, but do not uniquely determine, the qualitative organization used below. T0 is represented by skipped prerequisites, whereas T2 appears as incomplete outcomes, including failures involving domain-specific operations. P0 is divided into world-state and object-count inconsistencies. P2 is expressed through causal and boundary violations, manipulation and coupling failures, and mechanism violations. Physics N/A is not treated as an independent visual category because the relevant interaction is absent or otherwise unevaluable. F.2 SCOPE AND CASE SELECTION This appendix expands the qualitative analysis in the main paper with case-level visual evidence. We focus on recurring failure patterns identified during human review rather than enumerating every isolated rendering artifact. Our unit of analysis is goal-specific subgoal within generated video. Human-wrong control videos are excluded because they intentionally contain task failures while preserving physically valid human motion. Human-correct videos are used only as references when the expected action sequence, object affordance, or mechanism is not visually obvious. We select examples in which the required operation is unambiguous and the failure can be localized using evidence before, during, and after the relevant interaction. Each figure therefore includes the state preceding the error, the decisive transition, and, when necessary, an unobstructed frame after

We assign its primary category according to the first clearly observable violation and describe subsequent consequences as secondary errors. For example, skipped opening operation may later lead to an object crossing boundary that should remain closed, while an unexplained state change may enable an apparently successful final placement. The categories below describe observable video behavior rather than inferred internal causes. Less familiar objects or specialized affordances are therefore treated as possible contexts for failure, rather than as independent error categories. The selected cases illustrate recurring patterns and are not intended to provide an exhaustive taxonomy or an additional estimate of error prevalence. F.3 OVERVIEW OF ERROR CATEGORIES We organize the selected failures into task and physics categories, following the distinction used in the main paper. Task failures concern missing or incomplete operations relative to the requested goal, whereas physics failures concern inconsistent scene states or physically infeasible transitions. Table 17 summarizes the hierarchy used throughout the following sections. For each failure mode, we provide at least five representative examples in the subsequent analysis. The examples are selected to cover different goals and distinct visual manifestations, rather than repeatedly showing similar trials of the same task. They illustrate how each error appears in generated rollouts but do not enumerate all observed occurrences or provide an estimate of its prevalence. video may also exhibit multiple related errors. In such cases, the table and figures index the case by its primary failure, while secondary or downstream errors are described in the accompanying analysis. F.4 SELECTED EXECUTION EXAMPLES Task failures: required actions and outcomes. Some attempts proceed without establishing prerequisite state, such as cutting wrapped chocolate or pouring milk onto an inverted cup (Figure 11a). Others perform the action without achieving its required result: markings remain after wiping whiteboard, or toothbrush protrudes from travel case (b). Assembly errors show related distinction between manipulating the right objects and establishing the right relations, as when nesting dolls remain outside the largest shell or refill is placed in the wrong part of dispenser (c). These examples motivate checking prerequisites, action execution, and final states separately. Physics failures: continuity and interaction. Even recognizable task-directed actions can involve invalid physical changes. Figure 11d shows duplication and an object changing identity during handling. Panel (e) shows objects entering containers without an open access route, while panel (f) shows an incorrect laptop hinge axis and an invented hinge on nesting doll. Such errors motivate checks of continuity and interaction plausibility independently of task completion. Ordinary occlusion alone is not evidence of disappearance or penetration.

sections.content: Human rubric trade-offs. We test how the rubrics checks affect scores by removing gates and recomputing from fixed annotations (Figure 5). Removing T1 raises Task MAE from 0.292 to 0.497, and scoring the Task gates independently raises it to 0.306. Removing P1 raises Physics MAE from 0.432 to 0.922, while independent Physics scoring yields 0.777. These comparisons support retaining the initiation and continuity checks and the sequential gating. Table 18 reports all gate removals. These fixed-annotation comparisons test scoring rules, rather than whether different rubric would change what annotators observe. Different ablations answer different questions. The human rubric ablation recomputes scores from fixed observations and compares native Task or Physics scores with the mean of two independent holistic ratings, then averages MAE across rubric annotators. It does not rerun annotation. It uses pilot annotation study separate from the 600-video panel, in which annotators recorded every gate decision and, independently, holistic Task and Physics rating for each video. To test gating inside EGO2ACTJUDGE itself, we rerun the judge with its standard backbone and prompts on random subset of the human-rated panel, spanning all cases, and ask every Task gate (T1T3) for every subgoal and every Physics gate (P1P4) for every window instead of stopping at the first failure. Each videos answers are then scored twice, once with the sequential rule and once by counting all passed gates, so the two rules differ only in aggregation. The sequential scores reproduce the main run closely (Task = 0.91, Physics = 0.77 against the main run, and the same Final alignment with humans). Scoring gates independently raises the level of 9.1% of Task subgoals and 18.8% of judgeable Physics windows, and it lifts Final scores by 6.8 points on average. This inflation moves the judge away from the human consensus  (Table 19)  . Final drops from 0.69 to 0.65 and CCC from 0.62 to 0.51, and MAE rises on all three axes. Task and Physics correlations are unchanged, so the main effect is calibration: independent gates credit later checks that follow failed one, and humans do not. Plan stability. EGO2ACTJUDGE re-derives its Task and Physics plans from and f1 for every video, so the main run contains about 24 independent plans per case (2,558 plans over 109 cases, all distinct generations). Subgoal counts are stable: 91% of Task plans and 92% of Physics plans use their cases most common count, and in 88% (Task) and 86% (Physics) of cases the counts span at most one subgoal. Plans also name nearly the same objects (matched-subgoal F1 0.95 when only source and target objects are compared) but vary in wording and in how steps are split: requiring the same leading verb lowers F1 to 0.71 for Task and 0.61 for Physics (95% case-bootstrap intervals 0.660.76 and 0.580.64), lower bound because paraphrased verbs count as mismatches. Ordering constraints are the least stable part, agreeing for about 60% of matched subgoals that have prerequisite, but they do not enter the Task score. To test whether the Physics axis responds to known violations, we take 30 successful human recordings from different cases, each scored 100 on Physics in the main run, and create four versions of each: an unedited re-encode and three corruptions centred on the most active 3 of the video. Teleport deletes 1.5 of frames, swap reverses the order of two adjacent 1.5 segments, and ghost blends the frame from 3 earlier at 50% opacity for 2 s, so objects appear doubled. All edits exceed the 0.5 flicker exemption of the rubric. We judge all 120 videos with the standard configuration and compare each corrupted video with the rerun of its unedited version  (Table 20)  . No unedited video lost Physics points, and no corrupted video scored higher than its unedited version. Ghost duplication is detected in 55% of cases, almost always at the continuity gate P1, and lowers Physics by 30 points on average, while Task barely changes. Teleport and swap are detected in only 7% and 10% of cases. The Physics pass sees 24 evenly spaced frames, so 1.5 cut resembles an ordinary gap between samples, and the judge inspected the edited interval closely in only 7% (teleport) and 13% (swap) of videos. When it did inspect the ghost interval, it detected the duplication in 10 of 13 videos. Edits are placed by frame-difference energy, which can select camera rather than hand motion, and we do not verify that the failing window is the edited one, although the absence of false alarms makes spurious detections unlikely. sections.title: H LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE WORK
sections.content: Downstream use. EGO2ACT judges what generated rollout visibly shows, namely whether each subgoal is completed through physically plausible interactions, and it does not test whether rollout that passes actually helps downstream learning or planning. We see this visual check as necessary first step rather than sufficient one, since rollout that skips steps or breaks physics is unlikely to be useful for either, and it can be run at scale without robot or training loop. natural next step is to close this loop, for example by using EGO2ACTJUDGE as feedback signal for self-improvement in the spirit of VQQA (Song et al., 2026), which turns question-based video critiques into iterative prompt refinement, or by using it to rank rollouts and select training data. Scale of the human study. The human study rates 600 videos, which is sizable sample for measuring agreement, but they come from 25 of the 110 cases and so reflect only part of the benchmarks diversity. This is by design, as the study mainly serves to check the rubric against human judgment before the same rubric is turned into an automated judge, and EGO2ACTJUDGE then carries the evaluation across the full benchmark. Growing the study would still help, both by annotating more cases and by expanding EGO2ACT itself with more cases and domains. Longer tasks are another direction as native generation lengths grow, since we generate each rollout in single pass with the models own engine rather than with extension workflows such as ComfyUI (ComfyUI, 2023).

sections.title: Preprint
sections.content: Baseline adaptation and scope. Running existing evaluators on EGO2ACT meant adapting them to our setting, for instance mapping their outputs onto Task and Physics, serving the training-free ones through shared backbone, and rewording RBenchs robot-specific prompt for first-person video (Appendix C.2). We kept these mappings fixed and reported each methods native score alongside, but the adaptations may still not be the best fit for every method. We also leave out EgoForge (Shen et al., 2026) and EgoTV (Hazra et al., 2023), since EgoForge compares generations against reference videos, which would reward one recorded route over other valid ones, and EgoTV checks real recordings for task completion without looking at the physics of generated content. Working with the original authors on method-specific adaptations, or developing reference-free versions of egocentric evaluators, would make these comparisons broader and fairer.
